transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is... I got really worked up in a staff meeting the other day. I'm a personal care aide, you know, and we were talking about safety protocols, which is so important. I mean, just last week, my neighbor—he's this older guy, sweet as can be, always wearing those bright yellow suspenders—he tripped over his own garden hose. I told him he needed to coil it up, but he never listens. Anyway, in the meeting, I just started acting out a whole fall-prevention drill. I was moving chairs around, waving my arms to show how you're supposed to catch someone, and... I just couldn't seem to stop, even when folks were telling me to sit down. It was like I had to show them exactly how it works, you know? Just like I tried to show my neighbor, but he was more worried about his petunias getting crushed.
During that time you were acting out the drill, did you also notice your mood being unusually high, euphoric, or irritable, along with needing much less sleep than usual?

Yeah, I guess... there are these stretches where I just feel really bright and fired up, you know? Like everything is finally lining up. I had that going on when I was doing the drill. It's kind of like when I was reorganizing the supply closet the other day. Brenda—she's the shift manager at the facility—she buys these terrible, cheap wipes that just fall apart. I keep telling her you can't use those on the residents, their skin is like tissue paper. 

My Aunt Marie had skin like that before she passed. She used to collect those little ceramic frogs, had hundreds of them all over her living room shelves. Dusting them took hours, I swear, and if you chipped one she'd never let you hear the end of it. She bought most of them at yard sales... 

But anyway, I was feeling so good getting all the boxes in the closet stacked up perfectly by size, and then Brenda comes in and questions why I'm not doing my regular rounds. And I just... I snapped at her. Way harder than I meant to. It's like, if I'm in that zone and someone slows me down or questions me, I just lose my temper completely.

Have you ever had a period in the past—lasting a week or more—where you felt unusually depressed, low, or lost interest in things, or another time before this where you felt this same kind of high, energetic state?

Well, I mean... I don't really know if I've had a whole week like that before. I try not to keep track of the bad days, you know? It's like my old buddy Rick used to say—he was this guy I worked with back when I was doing construction, before I got into caregiving. Rick had this old beat-up Chevy truck, the thing was practically held together with duct tape and rust. He used to drive us out to this diner on Route 9 for lunch every Friday. They made the best meatloaf sandwich there, just smothered in gravy. The waitress, I think her name was Donna, she always remembered exactly how Rick liked his coffee—black, no sugar, but he always asked for a side of lemons for his water. Never understood that. But anyway, Rick always said, "Don't count the rainy days, just buy a better umbrella." So I don't really know if I've been low for a week straight, or high like this before. I just try to keep moving, you know? Like with the residents, you just gotta keep them moving or they stiffen right up.
Setting aside the high-energy periods, has there ever been a separate stretch of at least two weeks where you felt persistently sad, low, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Well... two weeks? I really don't think so. I mean, I don't think I've ever just sat around being sad for that long. It's like I was saying about keeping moving. You know, sitting still is the worst thing you can do. There's this one resident, Mr. Henderson—he's got this old recliner he brought from home, brown leather, cracked all down the armrests. He sits in it all day watching those old Westerns. Gunsmoke, Bonanza, you name it. The volume is always up so loud because his hearing aids are usually sitting on his nightstand. I keep telling him, "Mr. Henderson, you gotta put the hearing aids in," but he says they whistle too much. I tried to fix them for him once, just cleaning out the little tubes, but they're so delicate. Anyway, he sits there for weeks on end, and you can just see him fading. I couldn't do that. I couldn't just be low and not do anything for two weeks. I'd go crazy just staring at the wall like that.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive mood accompanied by increased goal-directed activity (spontaneously acting out a fall-prevention drill, reorganizing supply closet), pressured/tangential speech with flight of ideas (frequent unrelated tangents during interview), irritability with reduced frustration tolerance (snapping at coworker), and subjective sense of decreased need for rest while in this 'zone.'
